result.text: The paper tackles out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization by addressing a limitation of causal-invariance methods: they ignore whether features are not only invariant but also sufficient and necessary for predictions, so invariant yet insufficient features or sufficient but unnecessary ones can hurt robustness. The key insight is to quantify and favor features that are both sufficient and necessary using the probability of necessity and sufficiency (PNS), arguing that high-PNS features better capture stable causal mechanisms that generalize across domains. Methodologically, the authors define a PNS risk that scores representations by their PNS value, derive theoretical generalization guarantees linking low PNS risk to OOD performance, and implement an algorithm that learns representations maximizing PNS, validating it on synthetic and real benchmarks.

The paper addresses causal representation learning from high-dimensional temporal observations when real-world sampling rates are too slow to resolve fast causal interactions, creating effective "instantaneous" effects that break prior identifiability results. The key insight is that when interventions (e.g., agent actions) are observable, one can jointly learn a mapping from observations to multidimensional causal variables and a causal graph that permits instantaneous effects, restoring identifiability in intervened sequences. The proposed method, iCITRIS, uses a differentiable encoder to recover latent causal variables from temporal data while concurrently applying a differentiable causal discovery module that models both instantaneous and time-lagged edges conditioned on observed intervention targets; training is end-to-end on sequences with interventions to recover variables and their causal graph.

The paper addresses the problem of reliably estimating confidence for large language model (LLM) predictions, noting that many LLMs are poorly calibrated and resist standard post-hoc calibration techniques. Its key insight is that calibration can be derived from the model’s own behavior by measuring consistency across multiple stochastic generations: agreement among sampled answers serves as a proxy for true confidence. The authors propose three consistency-based measures computed from random generations, evaluate them across eleven models (open and closed) and nine reasoning datasets, and show these measures reduce calibration error compared to prior approaches; they also find that factors like intermediate explanations, model scale, and larger sample sizes improve calibration while instruction-tuning hinders it, and that consistency-derived confidence can even boost downstream performance, with practical guidance on picking metrics based on model traits such as instruction-tuning and RLHF exposure.

The paper addresses why large language models can perform in-context learning—adapting to a downstream task solely by conditioning on example prompts—despite not being explicitly trained to learn. The key insight is that when pretraining data exhibit long-range coherence governed by latent document-level concepts, the model implicitly learns to perform Bayesian inference over those latent variables, and at test time it applies the same inference to infer a shared concept across prompt examples, producing in-context learning behavior. The authors prove this mechanism in a formal setting where pretraining data are mixtures of HMMs, show that in-context learning can arise even with distribution mismatch between prompts and pretraining, and introduce a synthetic dataset (GINC) where Transformers and LSTMs empirically reproduce real-world phenomena (scale-dependent improvement, order sensitivity, and cases where zero-shot outperforms few-shot) predicted by the theory.

The paper examines Test-Time Adaptation (TTA), addressing the problem that inconsistent experimental settings and limited evaluations obscure the true robustness and limits of TTA methods under distribution shift. The key insight is that prior promising results hide three pervasive pitfalls—hyperparameter and model-selection sensitivity tied to online batch composition, strong dependence of TTA efficacy on the pre-trained model’s quality and properties, and the lack of any single method that reliably handles all common shift types even under ideal conditions. To demonstrate this, the authors introduce TTAB, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates ten state-of-the-art TTA algorithms across diverse distribution shifts and two protocols, and they run extensive experiments that reveal these failure modes and call for broader, more rigorous evaluations and a re-examination of underlying assumptions in TTA research.

The paper tackles hallucination in large multi-modal models (LMMs), where models produce image-inconsistent or instruction-inconsistent descriptions, by creating the first large, diverse visual instruction tuning dataset designed to train and evaluate robustness. The key insight is that including carefully constructed negative instructions—queries that prompt nonexistent-object claims, manipulations of existent objects, or incorrect knowledge—alongside positive examples forces models to learn to refuse or correct hallucinations and that a balanced mix improves robustness. Methodologically, the authors build LRV-Instruction (400k GPT-4-generated instructions across 16 tasks) containing both positive and three semantically distinct negative types, introduce GAVIE (GPT4-Assisted Visual Instruction Evaluation) to measure hallucination without human ground-truth, and finetune MiniGPT-4 and mPLUG-Owl on this dataset, demonstrating reduced hallucination and improved performance on public benchmarks.

The paper tackles the problem of online adaptation to continually changing test-time label distributions when true labels are unavailable, a common challenge for deployed ML systems facing nonstationary environments. The key insight is that even without observing true labels, one can still estimate the expected test loss well enough to reduce online label-shift adaptation to a standard online learning problem. Building on this, the authors adapt classical online algorithms—Follow The Leader and Online Gradient Descent—to update models using the loss estimates, prove regret bounds for these procedures, and empirically demonstrate that OGD in particular yields robust, effective adaptation across simulated and real-world label-shift scenarios.

The paper addresses the safety risk that LLM agents—especially those relying on long-term memory or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) knowledge bases—can be stealthily manipulated by poisoned memories or KB entries that cause malicious behavior when specific inputs occur. The key insight is that one can craft backdoor “triggers” not by changing model weights but by optimizing example texts so their embeddings map to a unique region of the retrieval space, ensuring those poisoned demonstrations are returned only when the trigger appears while leaving benign behavior intact. The method, AgentPoison, formulates trigger generation as a constrained optimization that selects or modifies poisoning instances to align their embeddings, injects them into the agent’s memory or RAG store at a very low poison rate, and then validates that triggered user instructions reliably retrieve the malicious entries; experiments show >80% attack success across varied real-world agents with <1% impact on benign performance and <0.1% poisoning.

The paper studies why invariance-based causal methods like invariant risk minimization (IRM) often fail at out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization for classification, asking whether the problem is method failure or a limitation of the invariance principle itself. The key insight is that, unlike linear regression where invariance can suffice, linear classification requires much stronger restrictions on distribution shifts and, even then, invariance alone can be insufficient—specifically when invariant (causal) features already encode all label information, spurious solutions can persist. To fix this, the authors show theoretically that combining an information bottleneck constraint with invariance eliminates these failure modes while preserving previous successes, and they operationalize this by proposing a learning objective that enforces both invariance across environments and a bottleneck on representations, validating its effectiveness empirically.

The paper tackles causal representation learning when observations are only partially informative—each measurement reveals a subset of latent causal variables and the observable subset can vary per instance—challenging standard identifiability assumptions that all latents are always reflected in data. The key insight is that an instance-dependent sparsity pattern in how latents mix into observations provides a principled constraint that enables identifiability: under either linear mixing with minimal assumptions or piecewise-linear mixing with Gaussian latents, the true causal factors can be recovered. Methodologically, the authors derive two theoretical identifiability results and develop two corresponding estimation algorithms that encourage sparsity in the recovered representations to match the partial-observability structure. Empirical results on synthetic and benchmark datasets show these sparsity-enforcing methods more accurately recover ground-truth latent variables than prior approaches.

The paper addresses the problem of producing interpretable, reliable confidence scores for large language model outputs by going beyond standard marginal calibration to ensure calibration across many intersecting subgroups. Its key insight is that forming meaningful groupings of prompt–completion pairs that are predictive of correctness—via embedding-space clustering and LLM self-annotation questions—enables multicalibration to correct systematic miscalibration that persists within subpopulations. The method adapts multicalibration algorithms to these groupings and introduces regularized algorithmic variants to reduce overfitting, then benchmarks these approaches across multiple QA datasets and models to demonstrate substantially improved fine-grained calibration and accuracy versus baseline confidence methods.

The paper addresses the theoretical gap in understanding how large pretrained language models can perform in-context learning—adapting to downstream tasks at test time by being given examples in their input without changing weights—by providing a PAC-style framework and finite-sample guarantees for this phenomenon. The key insight is that when pretraining data arise from a mixture of latent tasks, successful in-context learning primarily requires identifying which latent task generated the downstream examples rather than re-learning the task itself, so a fixed pretrained function can be combined with prompted examples to generalize. Methodologically, the authors formalize a two-phase model (pretraining that fits a function to a mixture distribution, followed by an in-context phase that appends labeled examples to inputs), and then derive sample-complexity bounds showing that under mild assumptions the latent task can be inferred and efficiently learned in-context despite distributional shift and frozen weights.

The paper addresses efficient test-time adaptation (TTA) under distribution shift, aiming to reduce per-sample computation and avoid catastrophic forgetting on in-distribution data. The key insight is that only a subset of test samples—those that are reliable and non-redundant—should be used for adaptation because high-entropy samples produce noisy gradients, and that constraining changes to important parameters prevents forgetting. The method actively selects low-entropy, diverse test samples to perform entropy-minimizing updates and applies a Fisher-based regularizer (with Fisher importance estimated from pseudo-labeled test data) to penalize large updates on critical parameters, yielding faster adaptation with lower backward-pass cost and preserved performance on in-distribution data.

The paper addresses out-of-distribution (OoD) generalization, where models trained on one distribution fail under varied real-world distribution shifts such as domain changes or spurious correlations. Its key insight is that separating category-related (causal) features from context-related (spurious) features and augmenting the latter can produce representations robust to multiple types of shifts. The method, DecAug, disentangles these factors by orthogonalizing gradients of category and context prediction losses with respect to intermediate features to isolate category- and context-related components, then applies gradient-based semantic augmentation on the context-related features to diversify and reduce reliance on spurious cues; experiments show this approach improves OoD performance across diverse benchmarks.

The paper tackles the problem of detecting knowledge hallucinations in LLM outputs, arguing that current token-level uncertainty or text-level self-consistency methods lose rich semantic information during decoding. Its key insight is that dense internal activations of LLMs retain semantic structure useful for judging response consistency, so analyzing these representations can better reveal hallucinations than post-decoding signals. The authors introduce INSIDE, which computes an EigenScore by measuring eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of response embeddings to quantify semantic consistency/diversity, and propose a test-time feature clipping technique that truncates extreme internal activations to reduce overconfident, hallucinated generations. They validate these methods with extensive experiments and ablations across multiple LLMs and QA benchmarks, showing improved hallucination detection performance.

The paper addresses robust test-time adaptation under distribution shift by detecting when a classifier’s predictive uncertainty (entropy) departs from the source distribution and adapting only when needed. The key insight is to monitor the stream of unlabeled test entropies with a betting-martingale-style detector and to adapt the model so that the test-time entropy distribution is driven to match the source entropy distribution, rather than simply minimizing entropy as in conventional self-training. Methodologically, the authors combine online betting/martingale change-detection with an adaptation update derived from a connection to optimal transport to construct a self-supervised loss that dynamically triggers and guides parameter updates; experiments show this improves accuracy under shifts while preserving calibration and performance when no shift occurs.

result.text: The paper tackles causal representation learning in a fully nonparametric, general setting where observed variables are arbitrary functions of latent causal variables and data come from multiple distributions (e.g., heterogeneous datasets or nonstationary time series) without assuming hard interventions. The key insight is that, by imposing a sparsity constraint on the latent causal graph and requiring suitable sufficient changes in causal influences across distributions, one can still identify structural information—specifically the moralized graph of the latent DAG—and link recovered latents to the true causal model up to specific component-wise ambiguities. Methodologically, the authors derive identifiability results showing how these sparsity and change conditions permit recovery of latent components and their moralized connections, characterize the nature of remaining nonidentifiability, and corroborate the theory with experiments that demonstrate recovery of most latent variables up to allowable transformations.

The paper tackles the fundamental problem of learning high-level causal variables and their causal graph from unstructured low-level observations (e.g., pixels), which is provably impossible from purely observational data; it asks what weak supervision is minimally sufficient for identifiability. The key insight is that paired samples obtained before and after unknown random interventions (but without labels about which variable was intervened on) provide enough structure—under mild assumptions—to identify the underlying causal representation and model. Methodologically, the authors formalize identifiability results for this weakly supervised setting and introduce implicit latent causal models realized as variational autoencoders that learn latent causal variables and causal mechanisms without explicitly optimizing discrete graphs; experiments on simple images and a robotic-manipulation dataset show these models recover causal variables and structure reliably.

The paper addresses how to separate aleatoric (data) and epistemic (model) uncertainty in large language models to improve reliability and interpretability when inputs are ambiguous or under-specified. The key insight is that generating and conditioning on multiple plausible input clarifications turns input-driven ambiguity into measurable aleatoric variability while residual disagreement across clarifications reflects epistemic uncertainty, enabling a decomposition analogous to Bayesian neural networks. The method, called input clarification ensembling, automatically produces a set of clarifying reformulations of a prompt, queries a pre-trained LLM on each clarified input, and ensembles the resulting predictions to compute separate aleatoric and epistemic components; experiments on several language tasks show this yields accurate and reliable uncertainty estimates.

The paper tackles how to reconcile tractable inference with a richly expressive hypothesis space to model human-like concept learning from few examples. The key insight is to factor learning into two stages—use a language model to generate natural-language hypothesis candidates, then apply Bayesian re-weighting with a learned prior and likelihood—thereby leveraging language as an expressive, enumerable hypothesis space while retaining principled probabilistic inference. The method estimates the prior from human data and evaluates the posterior-weighted hypotheses on tasks involving numbers and sets, covering generative, discriminative, propositional, and higher-order concepts, and shows that this hybrid approach predicts human judgments on diverse learning problems.

The paper tackles the failure of existing test-time adaptation (TTA) methods when unlabeled test data arrive as temporally correlated, non-i.i.d. streams (e.g., in autonomous driving) rather than the commonly assumed i.i.d. setting. The key insight is that adapting batch statistics and sample selection to account for out-of-distribution instances and class imbalance in the incoming stream can restore reliable adaptation under temporal correlation. Concretely, the authors introduce Instance-Aware Batch Normalization (IABN) to correct normalization for OOD or shifted samples and Prediction-balanced Reservoir Sampling (PBRS) to maintain a class-balanced reservoir that simulates an i.i.d. stream from a non-i.i.d. sequence, and they integrate these with TTA training updates. Experiments on several datasets, including real-world non-i.i.d. streams, show the method substantially improves robustness over prior TTA approaches while matching their performance in i.i.d. scenarios.

The paper addresses out-of-domain (OOD) generalization where models exploit spurious correlations that vary across environments, causing poor performance on unseen domains. The key insight is that by reweighting training data into mini-batches that are balanced with respect to spurious factors—thereby approximating a spurious-free distribution that reflects the invariant causal mechanism—one can recover Bayes-optimal classifiers that are minimax optimal across diverse environments. The method implements a causal balancing mini-batch sampling strategy grounded in a latent-variable data-generation model, provides identifiability results given sufficiently many training environments, and empirically outperforms 20 baselines on the DomainBed benchmark.

The paper addresses improving out-of-sample generalization by incorporating causal structure into neural-network regularization, motivated by evidence that predicting effects from causes yields lower test error than anti-causal learning. Its key insight is to jointly learn an input-layer-embedded adjacency matrix that represents a causal DAG and use that discovered causal graph to guide regularization, focusing reconstruction only on features with causal neighbors rather than reconstructing all inputs. The method, CASTLE, embeds a differentiable DAG adjacency matrix into the network, enforces acyclicity, and adds a reconstruction-based regularizer that reconstructs only causally connected features while training the predictor end-to-end; the authors prove a generalization bound and empirically show consistent out-of-sample improvements over standard regularizers on synthetic and real datasets.

The paper addresses the growing problem of hallucinations in generative image-restoration models, where visually plausible but incorrect details undermine reliability. Its key insight is that there is an information-theoretic tradeoff: as perceptual quality improves, the model's minimal achievable uncertainty necessarily increases, meaning perfect perceptual fidelity requires at least twice the problem's inherent uncertainty. Methodologically, the authors formalize inherent uncertainty for restoration tasks, prove quantitative relations linking uncertainty, perception, and distortion (deriving the perception–distortion tradeoff from the uncertainty–perception tradeoff), and validate the theory with experiments in super-resolution and inpainting. The results expose a fundamental limitation that practitioners must weigh when prioritizing perceptual realism versus reliable, low-uncertainty predictions.

The paper examines Test-Time Adaptation (TTA), addressing the problem that inconsistent experimental settings and limited evaluations obscure the true robustness and limits of TTA methods under distribution shift. The key insight is that prior promising results hide three pervasive pitfalls—hyperparameter and model-selection sensitivity tied to online batch composition, strong dependence of TTA efficacy on the pre-trained model’s quality and properties, and the lack of any single method that reliably handles all common shift types even under ideal conditions. To demonstrate this, the authors introduce TTAB, a comprehensive benchmark that evaluates ten state-of-the-art TTA algorithms across diverse distribution shifts and two protocols, and they run extensive experiments that reveal these failure modes and call for broader, more rigorous evaluations and a re-examination of underlying assumptions in TTA research.

The paper studies backdoor data poisoning—where an attacker injects a small set of watermarked, mislabeled training examples that cause models to misclassify any test input containing the watermark while leaving typical performance intact—and asks when and how such attacks are possible or preventable. The key insight is that a learning problem’s susceptibility to backdoors is governed by its “memorization capacity” (how many arbitrary label associations a learner can encode without hurting normal performance), and that detecting or removing backdoored examples is essentially equivalent to achieving robust generalization against such attacks. Methodologically, the authors present a formal theoretical framework and concrete constructions of successful backdoors to demonstrate attacker-favorable regimes, prove robustness results for settings with low memorization capacity, and analyze computational approaches showing that adversarial training can detect backdoors and that backdoor filtering and robust generalization are nearly equivalent tasks under reasonable assumptions.

The paper addresses the problem of identifying nonparametric, temporally causal latent variables and their time-delayed causal relations from nonlinear mixtures of observed sequential data, a setting where prior disentanglement results relied on restrictive functional or distributional assumptions. The key insight is that fixed temporal causal influences (time-delayed transitions) and modular distribution shifts provide side information that makes the underlying latent processes and their relations identifiable even when transitions and observations are arbitrary and nonparametric. The authors develop TDRL, a framework that models latent causal processes with time-delayed transitions, factorizes different types of distribution shifts (transition changes and observation changes), and learns a nonlinear mixing inverse to recover latent variables and their causal graph from sequential data under both stationary and shifted environments. Empirically, TDRL reliably recovers time-delayed causal influences and outperforms baselines that do not exploit the modular structure of temporal changes.

The paper tackles the problem of learning a shared causal latent representation and its causal graph from unpaired multi-domain data, where only marginal distributions per domain are observed and no cross-domain correspondences are available. The key insight is that, under a linear generative model, diversity across domains (e.g., varying interventions or mixing) provides enough constraints to render the joint latent distribution and the shared causal graph identifiable from marginals alone. The authors derive sufficient identifiability conditions for recovering both the joint distribution and the shared linear causal structure, and convert these theoretical conditions into a practical algorithm that estimates the shared latent factors and their causal adjacency by leveraging domain-wise distributional contrasts and linear de-mixing followed by causal discovery.

The paper tackles the problem of poor probability calibration in large language models (LLMs), especially after interventions like instruction tuning, which is compounded by LLMs' high compute cost and broad task versatility. The key insight is that calibration can be achieved more universally and efficiently by learning a lightweight auxiliary model from multi-task calibration data, rather than re-training or altering the base LLM itself. The proposed method, THERMOMETER, trains this auxiliary calibrator to take LLM outputs and task/context features as input and produce adjusted confidence estimates that preserve the LLM’s original accuracy while improving calibration on held-out and novel tasks. Empirical results across diverse benchmarks show THERMOMETER is computationally efficient and yields substantially better-calibrated responses across tasks without degrading model performance.

The paper studies how large language models can improve their own in-context learning abilities by using in-context learning recursively, a phenomenon the authors call meta-in-context learning. The key insight is that repeated exposure to task examples within the model's context can reshape its implicit priors and alter its in-context learning strategies, effectively allowing the model to adapt to a distribution of tasks without parameter updates. Methodologically, the authors analyze this effect in two idealized domains — one-dimensional regression and a two-armed bandit — showing how meta-in-context learning adjusts priors and strategies, and they validate the approach on a benchmark of real-world regression problems where it achieves competitive performance with traditional learning algorithms.

The paper tackles the problem of brittle test-time adaptation under domain shift caused by relying solely on either conventional batch normalization (CBN) or transductive batch normalization (TBN), where TBN’s dependence on large, i.i.d. test batches is often impractical and leads to failures at small or non-i.i.d. batch sizes. The key insight is that CBN and TBN form a trade-off and that layer-wise sensitivity to domain shift can guide an interpolation between source-derived (CBN) and test-batch (TBN) statistics to get the best of both worlds. The proposed Test-Time Normalization (TTN) computes a weighted combination of CBN and TBN moments per BN layer, with the interpolation strength determined by each layer’s domain-shift sensitivity, and can be plugged into existing test-time adaptation pipelines to stabilize normalization and improve robustness across batch sizes and realistic evaluation scenarios, yielding state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks.

The paper tackles why domain generalization (DG) methods fail inconsistently across different distribution shifts, especially when multiple attributes shift simultaneously, by arguing that trusting a single fixed regularization constraint is insufficient. Its key insight is that different types of distribution shifts correspond to different causal/independence constraints among observed variables in a canonical data-generating causal graph, so an algorithm must identify and impose the correct constraint for the particular shift to generalize. The authors formalize multi-attribute shifts with causal realizations, prove that no single fixed-constraint method can succeed across all shifts, and propose Causally Adaptive Constraint Minimization (CACM), which uses knowledge of the data-generating process to adaptively select and enforce the appropriate independence constraints; empirical results on synthetic and real datasets show adaptive, dataset-dependent constraints yield the best OOD accuracy while incorrect constraints hurt performance.

result.text: The paper tackles object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs), where models describe objects that are not present in images, undermining tasks like visual summarization and reasoning. The key insight is that hallucination arises from predictable statistical factors—object co-occurrence patterns, decoder uncertainty, and a tendency for hallucinated items to appear later in generated text—which can be exploited post-hoc to reduce false mentions. The authors propose LURE (LVLM Hallucination Revisor), a model-agnostic, post-processing algorithm that re-scores and reconstructs generated descriptions by accounting for co-occurrence priors, uncertainty signals, and positional cues to suppress unlikely objects. Evaluated on six open-source LVLMs, LURE yields about a 23% improvement on object-hallucination metrics and ranks highest in both GPT and human evaluations.

The paper addresses how to choose effective unsupervised losses for test-time adaptation (TTA), i.e., adapting a trained classifier to unlabeled test-domain samples under distribution shift. The key insight is that the best TTA loss for a given classifier closely relates to the convex conjugate of the supervised training loss: meta-learning over candidate TTA objectives recovers conjugate functions (e.g., a temperature-scaled entropy when the model was trained with cross-entropy), and the conjugate provides a principled local approximation to the original supervised loss that yields strong adaptation signals. Methodologically, the authors derive a generic recipe that computes the conjugate pseudo-label loss for any training loss in a broad class, interpret this as a form of soft self-training with conjugate pseudo-labels, and empirically show the resulting TTA objectives outperform entropy-based and other baselines across benchmarks and novel training losses like PolyLoss.

result.text: The paper tackles the fundamental ill-posedness of Causal Representation Learning (CRL), which aims to recover hidden causal variables and their relations from observational data but typically requires strong assumptions like temporal structure, interventions, or supervision to be identifiable. Its key insight is that identifiability can instead be achieved via a weak structural constraint on the observed mixing: observational variables can be partitioned into groups that each depend on only a subset of latent causal factors, and this grouping suffices to pin down the latent causal representation without temporal or interventional information. Methodologically, the authors formalize a generative model with grouped observational variables, derive identifiability results under these grouping conditions, and propose a self-supervised estimation framework tailored to the model; they prove statistical consistency and empirically demonstrate improved CRL performance and robustness to latent confounders and cycles compared to prior methods.

The paper tackles the problem of giving rigorous, distribution-free guarantees for generative language model outputs by adapting conformal prediction to the combinatorial, sampled-output setting of LMs. The key insight is to treat LM sampling as a sequential set-construction problem and jointly calibrate a stopping rule (when the candidate set is sufficiently likely to contain an acceptable answer) and a rejection rule (to remove low-quality samples), thereby producing small output sets that nevertheless contain at least one correct response with high probability. The method samples candidate responses, applies a statistically calibrated rejection test to filter noisy generations, and stops sampling according to a calibrated criterion that ensures coverage guarantees; it further extends the same calibration framework to identify smaller correct components (phrases or sentences) inside candidates. Empirically, this conformal language modeling approach yields compact, reliable candidate sets and component-level correctness guarantees across open-domain QA, summarization, and radiology-report generation with various LMs.

The key insight is that robustness requires screening out harmful inputs and stabilizing parameter updates: selectively adapting on high-confidence, class-uniform samples reduces the influence of outliers, while minimizing an entropy-sharpness objective guards parameters against destabilizing large gradients. The proposed method, SoTTA, implements input-wise robustness via high-confidence uniform-class sampling to filter test data and parameter-wise robustness through entropy-sharpness minimization during adaptation, and experiments on standard TTA benchmarks with various noisy conditions show SoTTA outperforms prior methods under noise while matching their accuracy on clean streams.

This paper addresses the longstanding question of how robustness relates to generalization by proving data-dependent generalization bounds that concretely tie robustness of a learned predictor on training samples to its generalization error. The key insight is that by basing the bounds on an observable, computable property of the training data rather than on worst-case hypothesis-space complexity or large covering-number factors, one can dramatically tighten guarantees and show robustness implies generalization in a data-dependent way. Methodologically, the authors derive new concentration inequalities for multinomial random variables and use them to obtain bounds that reduce dependence on covering numbers and eliminate explicit dependence on the hypothesis class, apply these bounds to examples like Lasso and deep networks, and validate near-exponential improvements both theoretically and empirically.

The paper studies why invariance-based causal methods like invariant risk minimization (IRM) often fail at out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization for classification, asking whether the problem is method failure or a limitation of the invariance principle itself. The key insight is that, unlike linear regression where invariance can suffice, linear classification requires much stronger restrictions on distribution shifts and, even then, invariance alone can be insufficient—specifically when invariant (causal) features already encode all label information, spurious solutions can persist. To fix this, the authors show theoretically that combining an information bottleneck constraint with invariance eliminates these failure modes while preserving previous successes, and they operationalize this by proposing a learning objective that enforces both invariance across environments and a bottleneck on representations, validating its effectiveness empirically.

The paper addresses object hallucination in grounded image captioning, where models produce words not supported by the visual scene due to misclassification or reliance on language priors. Its key insight is that aligning structural semantic information across modalities — i.e., enforcing consensus between a visual graph (scene graph) and a language graph that capture nodes and their relations — reduces semantic inconsistency and thus hallucination. The proposed Consensus Graph Representation Learning (CGRL) framework learns this cross-modal consensus representation by explicitly aligning nodes and edges of the visual and language graphs and injecting the aligned consensus into the grounded captioning pipeline so the model better captures both linguistic characteristics and visual relevance, then grounds generated object words to image regions. Experiments on Flickr30k Entities show CGRL substantially reduces hallucination (−9% CHAIRi) while improving captioning and grounding metrics (+2.9 CIDEr, +2.3 F1LOC) and human-evaluated quality.

The paper addresses efficient test-time adaptation (TTA) under distribution shift, aiming to reduce per-sample computation and avoid catastrophic forgetting on in-distribution data. The key insight is that only a subset of test samples—those that are reliable and non-redundant—should be used for adaptation because high-entropy samples produce noisy gradients, and that constraining changes to important parameters prevents forgetting. The method actively selects low-entropy, diverse test samples to perform entropy-minimizing updates and applies a Fisher-based regularizer (with Fisher importance estimated from pseudo-labeled test data) to penalize large updates on critical parameters, yielding faster adaptation with lower backward-pass cost and preserved performance on in-distribution data.

This paper addresses the lack of thorough, reproducible, and comparable evaluations in backdoor learning research, where rapid development and diverse experimental settings hinder tracking real progress. The key insight is that a large-scale, standardized benchmark combining modular implementations of both attacks and defenses and exhaustively evaluating their interactions is necessary to reveal realistic strengths, weaknesses, and factor effects. The authors introduce BackdoorBench, an extensible codebase implementing 8 state-of-the-art attacks and 9 defenses plus a standardized protocol, and run 8,000 systematic evaluations (all attack–defense pairs across 5 poisoning ratios, 5 models, and 4 datasets) to analyze performance under varied conditions. Their benchmark and public release of code and results enable reproducible comparisons, deeper empirical analysis of factors shaping backdoor success, and a foundation for future method development.

The paper examines whether Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) and related methods reliably achieve out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in classification by recovering predictors tied to invariant (causal) mechanisms when environments vary. Its key insight is that, under a broad and natural data model, IRM often fails: in the linear case simple conditions show IRM frequently does not recover the optimal invariant predictor, and in the non‑linear case IRM can fail catastrophically unless test distributions are already sufficiently similar to training ones. Methodologically, the authors analyze IRM and several alternatives formally—deriving conditions and counterexamples in linear settings and extending to non‑linear constructions that demonstrate failure modes—showing that these invariant objectives do not generally improve over standard Empirical Risk Minimization for OOD robustness.

The paper tackles identifiability in causal representation learning by asking when latent causal variables and their causal-polynomial relationships can be recovered from observed data across multiple environments, expanding beyond prior work limited to linear Gaussian models. Its key insight is that changes in causal influence parameters across environments—when combined with assuming polynomial structural functions and exponential-family noise—provide enough variation to uniquely identify the latent causal model (and under weaker conditions yield partial identifiability when some parameters remain fixed). Methodologically, the authors derive theoretical identifiability conditions for polynomial structural equation models with exponential-family noise, analyze cases of partial parameter change, and introduce an empirical estimation procedure motivated by these identifiability results; they validate consistency and the theory via experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.

The paper tackles the problem of producing informative conformal prediction sets when the target task has very limited training data, which otherwise causes prediction sets to inflate and lose usefulness. Its key insight is to view conformal prediction as a meta-learning problem over many exchangeable auxiliary tasks, leveraging transfer from those tasks to tighten prediction sets on the low-data target while preserving marginal coverage guarantees. The method uses a simple, fast, model-agnostic conformalization algorithm that learns calibration/meta-parameters across auxiliary tasks and then applies them to the few-shot target, and the authors validate this approach on classification and regression problems in NLP, vision, and chemistry, showing substantially smaller prediction sets without sacrificing theoretical coverage.

The paper addresses the understudied problem of "code hallucinations," where LLMs generate code that appears correct but fails to execute or meet requirements. The key insight is that hallucinations can be systematically categorized and detected via execution-based verification, yielding four primary types—mapping, naming, resource, and logic hallucinations—with finer subcategories to capture distinct failure modes. The authors introduce CodeHalu, a dynamic detection algorithm that runs and verifies generated code to classify and quantify hallucinations, and they construct CodeHaluEval, an 8,883-sample benchmark across 699 tasks to evaluate 17 popular LLMs, revealing substantial differences in generation accuracy and reliability and providing actionable diagnostics for improving code generation.

The paper tackles real-world test-time adaptation (TTA), specifically the challenge of adapting pretrained models at inference when the incoming data stream is non-i.i.d., undergoes continual domain shift, and is globally class-imbalanced. Its key insight is that indiscriminate adaptation of BatchNorm statistics biases models toward majority classes and that naive self-training, while useful for unlabeled data, over-adapts under continual shifts; combining a class-balanced normalization strategy with a regularized self-training scheme can therefore address both problems. Methodologically, the authors introduce Balanced BatchNorm to prevent normalization bias toward majority classes, adapt self-training for TTA but constrain model updates with an anchored loss to avoid catastrophic drift, and integrate these into a tri-net architecture called TRIBE that jointly leverages balanced normalization and regularized self-training. Empirically, TRIBE outperforms prior TTA methods across multiple datasets and protocols that emulate realistic imbalanced, non-i.i.d., and continually shifting test distributions.

The paper tackles the problem of stealthy dataset tampering: embedding backdoors into neural networks trained from scratch without ever inserting visible triggers into the poisoned training data. The key insight is that by crafting poisoning samples whose gradients and data selection mimic the influence of a true trigger during training, one can steer model learning so that a hidden trigger pattern later activates the backdoor even though the poisoned set contained no explicit triggers. result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of automatically optimizing LLM agents to use external tools and knowledge effectively, replacing brittle, manual prompt engineering that limits tool-assisted performance. The key insight is to train a comparator module that performs contrastive reasoning over positive and negative examples from training data to generate more informative, task-specific prompts that guide the agent toward correct tool use. Methodologically, AvaTaR iteratively samples example pairs, uses the comparator to synthesize insightful prompts highlighting distinctions between successful and failing behaviors, and refines the LLM agent on these contrastive prompts; evaluated on four multimodal retrieval and three QA datasets, this automated prompting loop yields consistent gains and strong generalization, improving Hit@1 by ~14% on retrieval and ~13% on QA.

The paper tackles the problem of when and how machine learning models can generalize to out-of-distribution (OOD) data by providing rigorous definitions and learnability criteria rather than relying on informal notions of invariance. Its key insight is that OOD generalization is governed by an "expansion function" that quantifies how much variance of features is amplified in test domains relative to training domains, which gives a precise, quantitative meaning to invariant features and shows that arbitrary OOD generalization is impossible without characterizing this amplification. Methodologically, the authors formalize OOD and learnability, introduce the expansion function, derive OOD generalization error bounds that depend on that function, and from the theory derive a principled model selection criterion; they validate this criterion empirically on benchmark OOD datasets, showing it outperforms baseline selection methods.

result.text: The paper addresses the surprising problem that combining ensemble methods and data augmentation—each known separately to improve accuracy, robustness, and calibration—can produce worse uncertainty calibration than using either technique alone. The key insight is that ensembles (which marginalize over weight configurations) and augmentation schemes that soften labels both introduce complementary forms of uncertainty reduction that compound into systematic under-confidence when combined. The authors analyze this pathology, show empirically that the combination creates a calibration–accuracy tradeoff, and propose a simple post-hoc correction that re-calibrates probabilities to counteract the compounded under-confidence. Applied to CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, the correction recovers both the accuracy benefits of combining methods and state-of-the-art calibration, outperforming using ensembles or augmentation in isolation.

The paper tackles the problem of selecting which training tasks to collect when building meta-learning systems under costly data acquisition, addressing the real-world sequential decision of how to gather task data to maximize downstream learning efficiency. The key insight is to frame active task selection as inference in a probabilistic latent variable model that captures both prior experience across tasks and uncertainty about task-related parameters, enabling principled, information-driven choices rather than random or fixed task sets. Their method integrates this probabilistic model into a meta-learning pipeline to score and select tasks sequentially—using joint posterior estimates to guide which tasks will most reduce uncertainty and improve future adaptation—and they validate the approach on simulated robotic benchmarks where it yields better data-efficiency than strong baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of poor out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization—particularly the tendency of distributionally robust optimization (DRO) and invariant risk minimization (IRM) to overfit when used with large overparameterized models. The key insight is that instead of constraining or changing the model, one can learn a model-agnostic reweighting of training samples so that standard empirical risk minimization on the weighted data yields robust OOD performance, and that searching over a low-complexity weight space (via a bilevel formulation) controls overfitting independently of model size. The method, called MAPLE, formulates a bilevel optimization where the outer loop searches for sample weights that optimize validation/OOD objectives while the inner loop trains the (potentially large) model on the weighted training data; theoretical analysis in linear settings shows MAPLE’s generalization is insensitive to model size, and experiments demonstrate substantial gains over prior state-of-the-art methods.

result.text: The paper tackles the vulnerability of test-time adaptation (TTA) methods to noisy, unexpected samples in unlabeled test streams—scenarios like unseen objects or corrupted inputs where existing TTA algorithms can be misled by blindly adapting to every incoming example. The key insight is that robustness requires screening out harmful inputs and stabilizing parameter updates: selectively adapting on high-confidence, class-uniform samples reduces the influence of outliers, while minimizing an entropy-sharpness objective guards parameters against destabilizing large gradients. The proposed method, SoTTA, implements input-wise robustness via high-confidence uniform-class sampling to filter test data and parameter-wise robustness through entropy-sharpness minimization during adaptation, and experiments on standard TTA benchmarks with various noisy conditions show SoTTA outperforms prior methods under noise while matching their accuracy on clean streams.

The paper addresses the vulnerability of deep neural networks to trojan (backdoor) attacks that are increasingly detected by defenses targeting simple, input-space triggers. Its key insight is that implanting a backdoor in deep feature space—by perturbing internal feature representations rather than relying on conspicuous input-space patches—yields triggers that are more effective, stealthy, controllable, robust, and harder for current defenses to detect. The method crafts a controlled “detoxification” procedure during training or fine-tuning that modifies feature activations to associate a chosen target label with inputs bearing subtle, learned feature-space signatures, and the authors validate this across nine image classifiers and multiple datasets (including ImageNet) to show the attack’s practicality and ability to evade state-of-the-art defenses.

args.text: I propose a rollback-safe, conformal control layer for test-time adaptation that wraps existing TTA updaters to provide finite-sample guardrails against harmful or unnecessary updates in non-i.i.d., class-imbalanced streams. The method uses the conjugate unsupervised loss matched to the training objective as a risk proxy and monitors its windowed distribution with a martingale-style detector, triggering updates only when the proxy risk significantly departs from source and predicted improvement clears an adaptive threshold. Updates are executed under a Fisher trust-region with class-balanced normalization and high-confidence, diverse sample selection, while maintaining shadow checkpoints that automatically roll back if the post-update proxy risk violates its conformal bound. This plug-in safety wrapper aims to cap false adaptations and forgetting with proxy-risk regret guarantees, while preserving gains under genuine shifts.

args.text: We propose Expansion-Calibrated PNS Learning (EC-PNS): estimate the expansion function over candidate representation dimensions across training environments and use it to reweight a probability-of-necessity-and-sufficiency (PNS) risk, prioritizing features that are both necessary/sufficient and minimally amplifiable under domain shift. Concretely, a domain probe estimates per-dimension expansion; the objective maximizes PNS under an information bottleneck while penalizing reliance on high-expansion features, preserving causal signal and suppressing pseudo-invariant components. Theoretically, if expansion is estimated within ε and the bottleneck is tight, we derive OOD error bounds that contract with the weighted PNS risk and avoid known IRM failure modes. Practically, EC-PNS can be plugged into DomainBed-style training by alternating probe and encoder updates, improving worst-domain accuracy over PNS-only or invariance+bottleneck baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses improving uncertainty quantification for deep classifiers by producing smaller, still-valid prediction sets from conformal prediction (CP) to enable safer deployment in high-stakes settings. The key insight is that leveraging a neural network’s learned representation to select and weight a local neighborhood of calibration examples yields more informative, input-adaptive calibration than the global, uniformly weighted CP approach. The proposed Neighborhood Conformal Prediction (NCP) algorithm finds k nearest neighbors in representation space for each test input, assigns importance weights based on distance, and uses these weighted calibration scores to form adaptive prediction sets; the authors prove that under mild conditions on the representation NCP yields strictly smaller sets than traditional CP and empirically validate substantial set-size reductions on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet across diverse architectures.

args.text: We propose order-aware sequential demonstration design for in-context learning. Building on the view that ICL performs Bayesian inference over latent tasks and mixtures, we cast demo selection as sequential Bayesian experimental design inside the prompt, selecting and ordering each next example to maximize information gain about the latent task for the target query distribution. We estimate this information with a small probe LM or amortized scorer and update it after each appended example; across prompts, we adapt the prior via meta-in-context learning to warm-start selection on future tasks. Unlike prior static one-shot demo selection, this method exploits order sensitivity and adapts online, targeting shorter prompts and better robustness under distribution shift.

Active-Robust Reservoir TTA (AR2-TTA): For temporally correlated, noisy test streams, maintain a prediction-balanced reservoir and restrict adaptation to high-confidence, diverse samples drawn from it, optimizing entropy with a Fisher-importance regularizer while applying per-layer CBN/TBN interpolation to stabilize small-batch statistics. Periodically issue a few active label queries—chosen via a scalable uncertainty-plus-diversity sampler—to recalibrate pseudo-labels and refresh Fisher estimates, preventing drift and catastrophic forgetting. This unifies reservoir balancing for non-i.i.d. data, robust sample screening, efficient/regularized TTA, and test-time normalization, targeting strong accuracy and stability across realistic batch sizes and shift conditions.

result.text: The paper addresses domain generalization, specifically failures of invariant risk minimization (IRM) for nonlinear classifiers and when pseudo-invariant features or geometric skews cause spurious solutions. The key insight is to cast invariant causal prediction in terms of mutual information and to enforce both invariance of predictors across domains and an information bottleneck that minimizes mutual information between inputs and learned representations, thereby suppressing pseudo-invariant features and geometric distortions. Methodologically, the authors derive a variational mutual-information formulation that yields a tractable loss for nonlinear models combining an invariance term (matching predictors across environments) with a representation-compression term (an information bottleneck), and they validate IIB on synthetic tasks and the DomainBed benchmark, showing improved robustness and average accuracy over IRM and other baselines.

The paper tackles the challenge of training reliable out-of-distribution (OOD) detectors when real OOD examples are unavailable and synthetic OOD data from generators can mistakenly overlap with in-distribution (ID) semantics, which confuses predictors. Its key insight is that these mistaken-but-generated samples can be repurposed to form an auxiliary OOD detection task that, if constructed so ID and auxiliary-OOD supports are disjoint and trained with a careful procedure, actually helps the model learn to separate true ID from OOD. The proposed method, Auxiliary Task-based OOD Learning (ATOL), generates candidate OOD samples, partitions them to create an auxiliary OOD class distinct from ID, and trains the predictor on both the main classification and the auxiliary OOD task with tailored objectives to mitigate the harm from mistaken generations. Experiments across multiple OOD setups show ATOL outperforms prior generation-based approaches by turning unreliable synthetic OODs into a useful training signal.

The paper tackles hallucinations in large vision-language models (LVLMs), where models generate incorrect or ungrounded text, without relying on costly extra data or doubling inference. Its key insight is that pretrained LVLMs can introspectively judge the importance of visual tokens conditioned on prior vision and text context, so selectively removing unimportant vision tokens early can amplify text-informed hallucination signals that reveal vision-text associations. The method, Self-Introspective Decoding (SID), uses a Context and Text-aware Token Selection (CT2S) strategy to prune unimportant vision tokens after early layers, computes amplified hallucination logits driven by the remaining vision-text association, and subtracts these from the original token logits during autoregressive decoding to suppress aimless visual hallucinations. Experiments show SID reduces hallucinations and improves text quality across metrics without extra knowledge sources and with minimal added computation.

The method fits performance-versus-mixture curves from small-scale experiments and combines them with standard scaling laws for model size and training steps to extrapolate how large models will behave under different mixtures, enabling selection of near-optimal mixtures and dynamic schedules; experiments show this approach recovers a superior mixture for a 1B model trained to 100B tokens (matching the effect of 48% more steps) and predicts critical mixture thresholds for continual training to avoid catastrophic forgetting.

The paper tackles the problem of maintaining zero-shot generalization of pre-trained vision-language models (like CLIP) without relying on task- or domain-specific training data that can hurt performance on unseen domains. Its key insight is that prompts can be adapted at test time using only the single test sample by enforcing consistency: a good prompt should yield confident, stable predictions across different augmentations of that sample, so optimizing for low-entropy, high-confidence outputs can tune prompts on the fly. args.text: We propose Counterfactual Occlusion Consistency Decoding (COCOD), an inference-time method that estimates causal visual grounding of each candidate token by measuring its logit sensitivity to batched counterfactual images where the top-k detected objects are selectively occluded. Using object masks from off-the-shelf vision models, we precompute encodings for the original and occluded views and penalize tokens whose semantics (e.g., noun mentions or relations) are not selectively sensitive to occlusion of the referenced region but are sensitive to unrelated occlusions. Coupled with introspective vision-token pruning to bound compute and post-hoc rescoring to suppress late-position errors, COCOD provides a training-free, model-agnostic reduction of object and relation hallucinations. This unifies external grounding cues with introspective decoding and principled rescoring, extending prior post-processing and token-suppression methods to a causal, counterfactual setting.

result.text: The paper tackles continual test-time adaptation (CTTA), where a deployed model must adapt to continuously changing unseen domains without catastrophic forgetting or excessive compute and parameter overhead, and extends evaluation beyond the usual disjoint-domain setting to more realistic gradual shifts. The key insight is that input-dependent, modular specialization via a small set of domain-specific low-rank experts plus learned routing can capture and reuse domain-adaptive knowledge efficiently, reducing forgetting while remaining lightweight. The method, BECoTTA, implements a Mixture-of Domain Low-rank Experts (MoDE) composed of multiple domain routers for selective, input-dependent routing and a Domain-Expert Synergy Loss that encourages strong dependency between inputs/domains and their expert modules; this design achieves superior adaptation on disjoint and gradual shifts with about 98% fewer trainable parameters.

The paper examines whether practical approximate machine unlearning techniques—designed to comply with data deletion requests—can also remove the effects of poisoned training examples, a desirable property for mitigating data poisoning attacks. The key insight is empirical: across a range of poisoning types (indiscriminate, targeted, and a new Gaussian poisoning attack), model architectures (image classifiers and large language models), and generous compute budgets, existing unlearning methods often fail to erase poisoning effects even when they appear effective by standard metrics. The authors introduce new poisoning-based evaluation metrics to more precisely quantify unlearning efficacy and show that, while some unlearning methods can modestly speed up removal compared to full retraining, they generally provide limited benefit and are not reliable substitutes for retraining unless provable guarantees are developed.

args.text: We propose APEX-CRL: identifiability of latent causal variables and mixed instantaneous/lagged graphs from temporally aliased sequences with asynchronous partial sensing and weakly labeled interventions. At each time step, only a random subset of views/sensors is active (instance-dependent sparsity), sampling is too slow so instantaneous effects may occur, and we observe intervention timestamps but not their latent targets. We show identifiability up to smooth reparameterization if the time-varying sensor masks satisfy a covering condition that, across pre/post-intervention windows, separates every latent pair under at least one mask configuration and interventions excite at least one affected latent across windows; this enables disambiguating instantaneous edges from mixing. We instantiate a mask-aware sequence encoder tied to an intervention-conditioned SCM with instantaneous and lagged edges, trained via a pre/post contrastive objective augmented with precision-geometry statistics to localize intervention-affected coordinates under unknown nonlinear mixing.

We propose Consistency-Conditioned Neighborhood Conformal Prediction for LLMs: a conformal framework that uses within-prompt self-consistency and local representation neighborhoods to produce compact, distribution-free candidate sets with coverage guarantees. For each prompt, we sample multiple stochastic generations (with optional chain-of-thought) to compute a consistency score and build a local calibration pool in explanation-embedding space; weighted nonconformity quantiles conditioned on this score yield tighter sets when the model is self-consistent and wider when not. To ensure fine-grained reliability, we apply multicalibration over learned prompt–completion groupings using the same covariates, and in low-consistency regimes we back off to entailment-set coverage for component-level guarantees. We hypothesize this hybrid reduces set size at fixed coverage versus prior conformal LLM methods, achieves subgroup-wise calibration, and surfaces aleatoric uncertainty via disagreement across automatic input clarifications.

Its key insight is that aligning the feature distribution of each OOD test sample to the source distribution via prompt adaptation reduces domain gap and yields more robust zero-shot performance. The method adapts multimodal prompts per test sample by optimizing prompt parameters to minimize a statistical measure of feature distribution shift (rather than only entropy), effectively performing test-time distribution alignment. Evaluated on domain generalization and cross-dataset benchmarks, this test-time prompt alignment improves zero-shot top-1 accuracy consistently over prior prompt-learning techniques.

The paper tackles why empirical risk minimization (ERM) often fails at out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization by reconciling contradictory findings about whether ERM learns useful invariant features or only spurious ones. The key insight is that ERM typically learns both invariant and spurious features but favors spurious ones when spurious correlations are stronger and, critically, downstream OOD objectives rarely learn new features—so the quality of ERM’s learned features becomes the bottleneck for OOD performance. To address this, the authors propose Feature Augmented Training (FeAT), an iterative procedure that preserves already learned features on one subset of data while forcing augmentation (learning new features) on another subset, thereby enriching the feature set available to OOD objectives. Experiments demonstrate that FeAT yields richer features and improves performance across several OOD methods.

args.text: Counterfactual Visual Evidence Decoding (CVED) is a training-free decoding scheme that suppresses LVLM hallucinations by demanding token-level visual evidence via counterfactual ablations. For each candidate noun or relational token, CVED identifies its supporting vision tokens via cross-attention/gradient attribution and contrasts the token’s logit under the original image with a counterfactual where those vision tokens are occluded or replaced by neutral features; a small evidence gap flags language-prior-driven hallucination and triggers penalties or blocking. To limit overhead and false positives, CVED bootstraps supports from open-source detectors and applies the test only to high-risk tokens, while calibrating penalties with a lightweight preference model trained on hallucinatory vs. correct token pairs. CVED unifies introspective token selection and preference-guided contrastive decoding into a causal, token-local grounding test that improves faithfulness without extra data or fine-tuning.

Change-Point Routed Reservoir CTTA (CPR-CTTA): Monitor the test stream with a composite betting-martingale over predictive entropy and class-marginal divergence to trigger adaptation only when a shift is statistically detected. Between events, maintain an instance-aware, prediction-balanced reservoir of high-confidence, diverse samples and update only normalization to remain stable under temporally correlated, imbalanced data. Upon a detected shift, route to (or instantiate) a lightweight low-rank expert and adapt it on the reservoir using the conjugate pseudo-label loss matched to the pretraining objective with a Fisher-regularized update, keeping shared parameters anchored to prevent forgetting. This yields compute-efficient, noise-robust CTTA with explicit false-alarm control and reusability across recurring domains.

CertRAG: a certified-robust retrieval and generation pipeline for LLM agents that mitigates memory/RAG poisoning by aggregating over randomized sub-indices. Inspired by BagFlip-style submodel ensembling, we build many memory shards via random bagging or hashing, run retrieval and re-ranking per shard, and apply a flipping-based aggregation rule that emits an answer only when a margin condition is met, yielding a certificate that up to t poisoned entries cannot alter the final answer. result.text: The paper tackles out-of-distribution (OOD) detection for pretrained classifiers by addressing the limitation of existing methods that rely on feature maps or full-gradient information without focusing on which model parameters are most relevant to in-distribution (ID) data. The key insight is that the directions most important for representing ID data lie in a lower-rank subspace, so OOD samples will produce gradients that are largely orthogonal to that subspace. GradOrth therefore computes gradients of a loss-related signal, projects those gradients onto the ID-important subspace (learned from ID data), and scores samples by the magnitude of their orthogonal (residual) component—large orthogonal norms indicate OOD. result.text: The paper tackles the persistent problem of hallucinations in instruction-tuned large vision-language models (LVLMs), where models generate non-existent objects, unfaithful descriptions, and incorrect relationships in visual question answering (VQA). The key insight is that existing evaluations focus mainly on object hallucinations and miss fine-grained unfaithful entity descriptions and relational errors, so a comprehensive, annotated dataset and targeted optimization can both detect and substantially reduce these multimodal hallucinations. The authors introduce M-HalDetect, a 16k-example dataset with fine-grained annotations for object, entity-description, and relationship hallucinations, and use it to train fine-grained multimodal reward models; they then apply Fine-grained Direct Preference Optimization (FDPO) to fine-tune InstructBLIP and employ best-of-n rejection sampling with the learned reward models. Human evaluations show these methods cut hallucination rates in InstructBLIP by 41% (FDPO) and 55% (rejection sampling), and the reward model generalizes to reduce hallucinations in other LVLMs (LLaVA and mPLUG-OWL), correlating well with human accuracy judgments.

args.text: CertRAG-Bagging provides provable robustness for retrieval-augmented agents against embedding-level memory poisoning by combining randomized sharded indices with flip-style ensemble aggregation, extending certified bagging concepts from classification to nearest-neighbor retrieval. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of providing finite-sample guarantees for prediction procedures that control not just set coverage but the expected value of arbitrary monotone loss functions (e.g., false negative rate, graph distance, token-level F1). The key insight is that the split-conformal framework can be generalized: by calibrating a scalar threshold on a monotone loss computed on a held-out calibration set, one can provably bound the population risk of the randomized prediction rule up to an O(1/n) tightness term. The method constructs risk-controlling prediction sets or rules by choosing the smallest threshold that yields the desired empirical risk on the calibration data and then applies that threshold to new inputs; the paper further extends this idea to handle distribution shift, quantile risk control, multiple and adversarial risks, and expectations of U-statistics, and demonstrates practical applications in vision and NLP.

The paper addresses understanding why prompt-tuning works for adapting large language models and specifically what role attention plays in enabling prompts to pick out task-relevant context. Its key insight is that softmax-based prompt-attention can be provably more expressive than both softmax self-attention and linear prompt-attention under a contextual mixture data model, and that gradient-based learning of the prompt can efficiently steer attention to sparse, context-relevant tokens with near-optimal sample complexity. Methodologically, the authors analyze a self-contained one-layer prompt-attention model: they provide expressivity separations, characterize the initial gradient-descent trajectory showing prompt and head recovery guarantees, and derive exact finite-sample performance when the prompt is known to quantify the precise benefit of context information. Empirical experiments on real datasets corroborate the theory by demonstrating that prompt-tuning causes the model to attend to context-relevant tokens and achieves the predicted performance gains.

The paper addresses robust test-time adaptation under distribution shift by detecting when a classifier’s predictive uncertainty (entropy) departs from the source distribution and adapting only when needed. The key insight is to monitor the stream of unlabeled test entropies with a betting-martingale-style detector and to adapt the model so that the test-time entropy distribution is driven to match the source entropy distribution, rather than simply minimizing entropy as in conventional self-training. Methodologically, the authors combine online betting/martingale change-detection with an adaptation update derived from a connection to optimal transport to construct a self-supervised loss that dynamically triggers and guides parameter updates; experiments show this improves accuracy under shifts while preserving calibration and performance when no shift occurs.

result.text: The paper addresses how well risk-sensitive learning—where one minimizes a risk measure of loss rather than its expectation—generalizes from finite samples, focusing on optimized certainty equivalents (OCE) that capture many common risks (entropic, mean-variance, CVaR). The key insight is that OCEs admit both a Rademacher-complexity-based generalization bound that unifies and tightens prior results (including for expected loss and CVaR) and a novel variance-based characterization that yields expected-loss guarantees with weaker dependence on the OCE’s smoothness. Methodologically, the authors derive two complementary learning bounds for empirical OCE minimizers—one via uniform convergence using Rademacher averages of the hypothesis class and another by relating OCE deviations to variance terms—and validate the bounds’ implications through exploratory neural network experiments.

The paper addresses domain generalization, specifically failures of invariant risk minimization (IRM) for nonlinear classifiers and when pseudo-invariant features or geometric skews cause spurious solutions. The key insight is to cast invariant causal prediction in terms of mutual information and to enforce both invariance of predictors across domains and an information bottleneck that minimizes mutual information between inputs and learned representations, thereby suppressing pseudo-invariant features and geometric distortions. Methodologically, the authors derive a variational mutual-information formulation that yields a tractable loss for nonlinear models combining an invariance term (matching predictors across environments) with a representation-compression term (an information bottleneck), and they validate IIB on synthetic tasks and the DomainBed benchmark, showing improved robustness and average accuracy over IRM and other baselines.

result.text: The paper addresses Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) under realistic, dynamic domain shifts where target domains recur with varying frequencies and short, unpredictable durations—conditions in which existing methods that adapt the same model parameters struggle with slow convergence, forgetting, or wrong reuse of past adaptations. The key insight is that maintaining a compact, editable set of domain-specific visual prompts (a "prompt coreset") and selectively updating or reusing them based on similarity lets the model quickly align to brief revisits while preserving past knowledge without retraining full parameters. DPCore implements this by combining visual prompt adaptation for lightweight alignment, a prompt coreset that stores representative prompts for past domains to prevent forgetting, and a dynamic update mechanism that edits close prompts or adds new ones when incoming domains differ substantially; this yields state-of-the-art CTTA performance across benchmarks while cutting trainable parameters by 99% and compute by 64%.

The paper addresses the security risk that adversaries can exploit selective forgetting (machine unlearning) requests to maliciously manipulate or degrade a trained model instead of legitimately removing data. Its key insight is that unlearning mechanisms can be attacked either statically—by submitting a batch of engineered deletion requests up front—or sequentially—by issuing requests over time—where the latter can be framed as a stochastic optimal control problem to maximize model damage while evading detection. The authors develop optimization algorithms to construct effective malicious update requests for both static and sequential settings, provide theoretical analysis of attack efficacy, and validate their methods empirically to show these attacks can substantially alter model behavior without retraining from scratch.

The paper tackles out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization by addressing a limitation of causal-invariance methods: they ignore whether features are not only invariant but also sufficient and necessary for predictions, so invariant yet insufficient features or sufficient but unnecessary ones can hurt robustness. The key insight is to quantify and favor features that are both sufficient and necessary using the probability of necessity and sufficiency (PNS), arguing that high-PNS features better capture stable causal mechanisms that generalize across domains. Methodologically, the authors define a PNS risk that scores representations by their PNS value, derive theoretical generalization guarantees linking low PNS risk to OOD performance, and implement an algorithm that learns representations maximizing PNS, validating it on synthetic and real benchmarks.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of adapting vision-language models at test time to improve robustness on challenging, unlabeled images without costly online fine-tuning. Its key insight is that a near-optimal episodic test-time adaptation procedure can be obtained simply by taking multiple augmentations, keeping only the most confident predictions, and marginalizing with a zero-temperature (argmax) softmax—an approach they call ZERO—which dispenses with gradient updates and heavy prompt tuning. Methodologically, ZERO performs N augmentations per test image, runs a single batched forward pass through the vision encoder, selects the top-confidence class predictions across augmentations, and aggregates them via zero-temperature marginalization to produce a final label. Empirically, ZERO matches or outperforms prior prompt-tuning TTA methods while being about an order of magnitude faster and significantly more memory-efficient, making it a strong, simple baseline for future TTA work.

args.text: We propose Discover-and-Align with Necessity Bottleneck (DANB), an environment-free OOD training scheme that synthesizes pseudo-environments via label-preserving augmentations optimized to maximize between-group gradient covariance divergence, then aligns them with a Fishr-style gradient-variance matching regularizer. To suppress pseudo-invariant or unnecessary features, DANB adds an information-bottleneck term whose per-feature penalties are adaptively weighted by estimated probabilities of necessity and sufficiency (PNS) obtained via counterfactual occlusion/perturbation probes on the learned representation. This yields a multi-objective optimization balancing ERM, invariance alignment, and necessity-weighted compression without requiring known domain labels. We hypothesize that discovering hard pseudo-environments and prioritizing high-PNS features closes known IRM failure modes in nonlinear classification while preserving the benefits of invariance-plus-bottleneck objectives.

Interventional Bottleneck with Necessity–Sufficiency (IB-NS) for OOD generalization. We estimate per-feature probabilities of necessity and sufficiency (PNS) via counterfactual-style latent perturbations and learn a representation Z that maximizes aggregate PNS while enforcing an information bottleneck and cross-environment invariance. Concretely, we use gradient-orthogonalized disentanglement to separate category from context features, then apply a FeAT-style two-split schedule that preserves current high-PNS invariants on one split while forcing augmentation to discover new causal features on the other, with PNS re-estimated each round. This jointly prunes pseudo-invariant or redundant features and expands missing causal ones, aiming to outperform ERM/IRM variants under spurious correlations, domain, and geometric shifts.

result.text: The paper tackles hallucination in large multimodal models—erroneous text output that is inconsistent with visual input—by proposing a decoding-time fix rather than retraining. The key insight is to use the model’s own detailed, self-generated descriptions of the image as contrastive references: comparing candidate continuations against those descriptions helps identify and suppress tokens that deviate from the actual visual content. The method, COuntering DEscription Contrastive Decoding (CODE), computes token-level adjustments during decoding by dynamically reweighting next-token probabilities based on similarity to the self-generated description versus the primary prompt-conditioned distribution, thereby steering generation toward outputs aligned with the visual counterpart. CODE is a plug-in contrastive decoding strategy that requires no extra training and empirically reduces hallucinations and improves cross-modal consistency across multiple benchmarks.
